title: Thermomigration columns replace etched copper TSVs in memory stacks
idea: Use the 1970s GE temperature-gradient zone-melting process. Before any front-end processing, print 10 um Al dots on n-type wafers at TSV sites and drive them through 60 um of silicon under a ~50 C/cm gradient at ~1100 C. Each dot leaves a recrystallized, junction-isolated p+ column that later serves as a via once the finished HBM core die is thinned to expose it.
why: Fact 6: removes DRIE, liner, barrier/seed, Cu plating, CMP and the reveal steps behind the HBM TSV tax and its 20-30% yield loss, using a batch furnace step with no critical mask. The risk is ~30 ohm per column and junction capacitance, so columns are bundled for power.

title: Head-per-track drum streams LLM weights at HBM-class bandwidth
idea: Revive the 1955 IBM 650 head-per-track drum: a glass-platter rotor read by fixed multi-channel head arrays (tape-drive-style heads built on AlTiC ceramic wafers) streams every stored weight once per revolution, matching LLM decode, which reads all weights once per token.
why: About 1,000 parallel channels x ~2.5 MB per track x 120 rev/s = ~300 GB/s from non-volatile magnetic media at cents per GB, with no silicon wafer in the storage medium; frees HBM for KV-cache.
note: Fixed-head magnetic drum streams all weights once per token; head-array cost and per-drum capacity are doubts.

title: A pixel kept dark is a memory: pinned-well cells from image-sensor fabs
idea: Paradox: an image sensor in permanent darkness is a near-leakless memory. The storage element is a CMOS-image-sensor pinned well (charge buried under a p+ pinning layer so surface states are filled), written and read through a transfer gate plus source follower like a light-shielded global-shutter pixel, with charge transferred back after reading.
why: Pinned wells show dark currents ~1e-18-1e-17 A vs ~1e-14 A DRAM tail, giving second-scale retention and near-zero refresh; made in mature, U.S.-present CIS fabs without EUV; best for refresh-dominated capacity tiers despite ~4-8x larger cell.
note: CIS pinned wells give long retention in non-EUV fabs; 4-8x larger cell hurts cost/bit.

title: GHz gate reflectometry reads a gain cell with no DC path
idea: Instrument: the RF gate reflectometry used for spin-qubit readout, where a storage node gates a minimum-size MOS varactor whose capacitance changes ~3x between depletion and inversion and an LC-resonant read line detects the resonance shift. Memory it unlocks: a gain cell where only the write switch touches the storage node, read non-destructively with no DC current, so reads never need restore and the read path adds no leakage or disturb.
why: Refresh and access energy: reads skip restore (~half of activate energy), and the single write switch can be long-channel for ~10x lower leakage per cell.
note: Qubit RF readout as DC-free gain-cell read; per-line resonator cost.

title: Forget activations, check them backward: reversible-network dual reconstruction
idea: Paradox: not storing data supplies the redundancy that checks stored data. In reversible networks each layer's input can be read from SRAM or reconstructed exactly from its output; storing a subset of activations and reconstructing the rest gives two independent derivations of overlapping tiles, and mismatching tiles are replaced by the reconstruction.
why: Activation memory down ~2-10x plus ECC-free error detection/correction for SRAM-resident activations on capacitorless accelerators; ~25-30% extra backward compute.
note: Reuses RevNet reconstruction as redundancy; floating-point drift complicates exact comparison; coverage only on stored layers.

title: OOM-as-migration lets schedulers allocate predicted, not requested, memory
idea: Stack 'jobs get only their predicted median footprint' with 'zero OOM kills': when a container nears its cgroup limit, the node agent freezes it, takes a CRIU checkpoint to local NVMe and restores it on a host with free memory (or raises the limit if the host has room), so safety padding in memory requests becomes unnecessary.
why: Batch, HPC and Kubernetes memory requests average 2-3x actual use; a transparent escape hatch raises cluster memory utilization 1.5-2.5x.
note: CRIU escape hatch lets requests be median-sized; migration latency is the doubt.

title: Successive-approximation bit-plane tiers: read MSB tier first, stop early
idea: Like a 1950s successive-approximation converter, store each tensor value's bits in separate tiers (one bit-plane per tier) and read MSB tiers first; the accelerator stops when the partial value already decides the outcome (ReLU negative, outside top-k, far below softmax max).
why: Average bits fetched per value drop from 8-16 to ~2-4 on many inference loads, cutting access energy up to ~4-8x and bandwidth.
note: Early-termination bit-serial inference is known; mapping bit-planes to tiers is the new part.

title: Memory built to forget: millisecond-retention tier needs no high-k pillars
idea: Add a DRAM tier specified for only ~1 ms retention at 85 C, where the runtime places only short-lived data (activations, KV-cache scratch, network buffers, GC nurseries) and refreshes only live pages. With retention relaxed 64x, a planar or shallow-trench SiO2/Si3N4 capacitor of ~0.5-1 fF on short bit-lines suffices, so the forgetting is the spec, not a defect.
why: For a large share of bits it removes HfO2/ZrO2 ALD, TiN plates, 60-75:1 capacitor etch with its fluorocarbon gases, and the carbon hardmask. The cell process nears logic-fab simplicity, cutting capacitor-module cost and materials ~70%.
note: Software placement plus planar caps; 64x refresh rate on live pages erodes energy gains.

title: Memory made by non-memory industries: open substrate-agnostic thin-film PDK
idea: Fund an open thin-film memory process design kit and qualification suite whose cell (low-temperature TFT plus planar or rolled capacitor) is defined by electrical windows rather than by substrate. Steel-coil coaters, battery-foil makers, disk-media sputter houses and PV lines can then certify as memory foundries on their own substrates, so the memory industry grows by not needing a memory fab.
why: Unlocks large, depreciated, partly U.S. coating capacity and non-silicon substrates for capacity-tier memory, cutting capital per added bit ~10x versus a DRAM fab. Device performance gates which tiers it serves.
note: Executable policy unlocking coating capacity, but TFT performance restricts it to capacity tiers.

title: Weaker write path, stronger retention: series-stacked gain-cell write transistors
idea: Paradox: a slower write device yields a stronger hold. In a capacitorless 2T gain cell (storage node = read-FET gate) the write device is split into two series transistors on separate gates, both pulsed on to write; in hold the middle node self-biases the upper device to negative VGS (stack effect), and a leakage-tail outlier now needs both devices defective at once.
why: Tail probability p becomes ~p^2 (e.g. 1e-5 to 1e-10 of cells below spec) plus ~10x nominal leakage cut, removing retention profiling and stretching refresh 10-100x with no capacitor.
note: Stack-effect leakage cut is known; p^2 tail assumes independent per-device defects, plausible for random traps.

title: Insulator made denser by conductor: metal-island percolation dielectric capacitors
idea: Build the capacitor dielectric as an Al2O3 or SiO2 matrix loaded with isolated 1-2 nm aluminum or TiN nano-islands (sub-monolayer metal cycles in a nanolaminate) tuned just below the percolation threshold. Near percolation the effective permittivity climbs steeply to k 50-100+ as islands form a dense series-parallel micro-capacitor network: conductors make the insulator better.
why: High-k without Hf/Zr, from abundant Al, Si, O and Ti. k~70 relaxes the capacitor aspect ratio from ~70:1 toward ~40:1 (fact 1), cutting etch-gas and hardmask use. Leakage near percolation is the risk.
note: Near-percolation k comes with leakage and dispersion at ns speeds.

title: Lossy AND bit-exact: Freivalds-certified 3-bit weights with flash fallback
idea: Serve from 3-bit resident weights while keeping, per matrix, a few exact random projections r^T W (one n-vector each); every step measures the true projected output error r^T(W - Wq)x on the live input, and when the top-1 logit margin exceeds the certified error the token matches FP16 decoding with probability 1-delta. Only low-margin steps rerun with exact weight blocks fetched from flash.
why: ~5x less weight DRAM while greedy outputs match full precision on certified steps; expected fallback under 5% of steps, so flash bandwidth stays modest.
note: Freivalds projections to gate flash fallback; single projection does not bound logit error through nonlinear layers.
